definition.text: Acid rain is rain, snow or other precipitation that is unusually acidic, with a low pH.

facts.text: Most water has a pH between 6.5 and 8.5, while acid rain averages about 4–5; one definition sets the line at a pH below 5.
Burning fuels and smelting ores release sulfur dioxide and nitrogen oxides, which reactions in the air turn into sulfuric and nitric acid.
Today's acid rain comes mainly from human sources such as coal-fired power stations, animal farming, fertilizers, steel mills and vehicles.
Power plants produce a quarter of the nitrogen oxides and two-thirds of the sulfur dioxide in the air.
Fossil fuels and industry emit 70 Tg of sulfur a year as SO2, against 2.8 Tg from wildfires and 7–8 Tg from volcanoes.
In 1852 Robert Angus Smith first linked acid rain to air pollution, in Manchester.
Heavily affected regions include eastern Europe into Scandinavia, the eastern third of the United States and southeastern Canada.

definition.text: Acid deposition is the delivery of acids from the air to the ground, either washed down by precipitation (wet) or settling without it (dry).

facts.text: Wet deposition happens when rain, snow or fog carries acids down to the surface.
Dry deposition, when particles and gases stick to ground, plants or other surfaces, can make up 20 to 60% of total acid deposition.

definition.text: Acid rain harms forests, fresh waters and soils, kills plants and animals, damages buildings and affects human health.

facts.text: Lower pH and more aluminium in surface water harm fish, other aquatic animals, microbes and plants.
Below pH 5 most fish eggs will not hatch, and below pH 4 adult fish die.
Acid kills sensitive soil microbes and disables their enzymes, causing soil functions such as decomposition to collapse.
High-altitude forests are especially vulnerable because the clouds and fog around them are more acidic than rain.
Acids react with limestone and marble in buildings and statues to form gypsum, which flakes off.
Breathing pollutants linked to acid rain, such as nitrogen dioxide, can damage the respiratory tract.

definition.text: Acid rain has been reduced by scrubbing sulfur from power-station exhaust, international treaties and emissions trading.

facts.text: Flue-gas desulfurization removes 95% or more of the SO2 from a typical coal-fired station's exhaust.
Under the 1979 Convention on Long-Range Transboundary Air Pollution, sulfur and particle emissions fell 30-80% in Europe and 30-40% in North America since 1990.
In emissions trading, each polluter holds allowances for its emissions and can sell those it no longer needs after installing controls, giving an economic incentive to cut pollution.
The first emissions trading market was created by the US Clean Air Act Amendments of 1990 to cut SO2 at the lowest cost to society.

definition.text: Brownfield land is previously developed land, abandoned or underused, that may be polluted from past industrial use.

facts.text: Definitions vary by country, mainly over whether contamination must be present.
Examples include abandoned factories, ash ponds, landfills, dry cleaners and gas stations.
Typical contaminants are spilled hydrocarbons, solvents, pesticides, asbestos and heavy metals such as lead.
The US is estimated to have over 500,000 brownfield sites contaminated below Superfund level.
The term was first used at a US congressional field hearing on June 28, 1992.
Industrial brownfields can be valuable ecosystems supporting rare plants, animals and invertebrates.
Redeveloping brownfields has become a key part of large urban greening projects.

definition.text: Valuing a brownfield needs specialised appraisal, because contamination changes a site's best use and value before and after cleanup.

facts.text: The value should allow for lingering stigma and possible liability to third parties.
Normal appraisal often fails, so appraisers use contingent valuation, case studies or statistical analysis.
A 2014 study of EPA cleanup grants from 2002 through 2008 found an average benefit of almost $4 million per site, with a median of $2.1 million.
Some environmental firms team up with insurers to guarantee cleanup costs.

definition.text: Many contaminated brownfields sit unused for decades because cleaning them costs more than the land would then be worth.

facts.text: Brownfields carry an environmental stigma that can delay redevelopment.
The US Superfund law has been criticised for pushing investment to greenfields through severe no-fault liability.
Redevelopment grew in the 2000s as developable land became scarcer in crowded areas.
Governments offer help: the EPA awarded nearly 1,000 cleanup grants worth almost $190 million from 2002 through 2013, and cleanup costs are fully tax-deductible.

definition.text: Brownfield remediation is cleaning contaminated former industrial land so it can be reused.

facts.text: Techniques include heating soil in place, bioremediation, in situ oxidation and soil vapour extraction, often combined.
Binders can be mixed into soil to stop chemicals leaching.
Phytoremediation uses deep-rooted plants to draw heavy metals out of the soil.

definition.text: Hazardous waste is waste that can damage human health or the environment.

facts.text: Waste can be hazardous because it is toxic, reactive, corrosive or ignitable.
As of 2022, humanity produced 300–500 million metric tons of hazardous waste a year.
Common sources include solvents, batteries and by-products of metal refining.
Many ordinary businesses, such as dry cleaners, car repair shops, hospitals and photo labs, generate it.
Mismanaged hazardous waste can pollute the air, raising illness and death, and contaminate groundwater and soil.
It is regulated at local, national and international levels.

definition.text: Hazardous waste is disposed of by treating and stabilising it for secure landfills, burning it, or recycling it.

facts.text: Incinerators burn it at 870–1400 °C, greatly shrinking it, but the leftover ash and gases can also be hazardous.
Some hazardous materials, such as lead–acid batteries and circuit boards, can be recycled into new products.
Landfills for such waste need barriers along their foundations to stop groundwater contamination.
Plasma treatment above 3000 °C turns waste into inert rock-like slag; it is very expensive but suits persistent pollutants such as PCBs.

definition.text: Poorer people and social minorities face a higher risk of exposure to hazardous waste and its pollution.

facts.text: An Austrian study found people living near industrial sites are more often unemployed, less educated and twice as likely to be immigrants.
Groups who rely on local land and streams for food and water, including Native Americans, face multiplied risk.

definition.text: Hazardous waste has been shipped from rich countries to poorer ones with weaker rules, prompting the Basel Convention to curb the trade.

facts.text: As laws such as RCRA raised disposal costs in developed nations in the 1970s, the waste trade to poorer countries grew fast.
In 1990 OECD countries exported around 1.8 million tons of hazardous waste.
199 countries signed the 1992 Basel Convention to stop this flow.
UN Sustainable Development Goal 12 includes sound management of chemicals and wastes throughout their life cycle.

definition.text: A landfill is a site for disposing of waste, including household rubbish.

facts.text: It is the oldest and most common way of disposing of waste, though systematic burial with daily and final covers only began in the 1940s.
The modern sanitary landfill is an engineered facility that separates and confines waste, widely adopted in the 1960s and 1970s to end open dumps.
Landfills take up much land and pose environmental risks such as groundwater and soil contamination.
Nuisances include dust, odour, noise, disease-carrying rats and flies, and lower local property values.
Permitting a US landfill generally takes five to seven years and costs millions of dollars.
Closed landfills are often reused as parks, bike courses or solar farms.

definition.text: A sanitary landfill works as a biological reactor in which microbes break organic waste down into simpler, less toxic compounds over several phases.

facts.text: First, oxygen trapped in the waste supports aerobic breakdown until microbes use it up.
In the acid phase, fatty acids build up and leachate pH falls from about 7.5 to 5.6.
In the longest phase, methane-making microbes turn the acids into methane and CO2.
Finally methane production almost stops as nutrients run short and oxygen seeps back in.

definition.text: Leachate is the contaminated liquid formed when water seeps through landfill waste, picking up organic matter, heavy metals and other pollutants.

facts.text: If not contained, it can contaminate groundwater.
Modern landfills use impermeable liners several metres thick, stable sites and collection systems to capture it.
Full landfills are sealed to stop rain entering and forming new leachate.

definition.text: Landfill gas is the mix of mainly methane and carbon dioxide produced when microbes digest organic waste without oxygen.

facts.text: On average it is about half methane and slightly less than half CO2.
Landfills are the 3rd largest emitter of methane worldwide.
Well-managed landfills collect the gas, either flaring it or using it to generate electricity; more than 850 US landfills recover it.
Capturing landfill methane is a common type of carbon offset project.

definition.text: Aftercare is the long period after a landfill is full and capped, when liners, gas capture and leachate treatment continue to limit harm.

facts.text: Aftercare may last from several decades up to forever, costing more than 20 million euros per landfill in the Netherlands.
Because sealed waste keeps its power to pollute, replacing liners and treating leachate is an indefinite requirement.

definition.text: Alternatives to landfill include waste reduction and recycling, waste-to-energy incineration, anaerobic digestion, composting and other treatments.

facts.text: Depending on local economics and incentives, these can be made cheaper than landfilling.
Germany, Austria, Sweden, Denmark, Belgium, the Netherlands and Switzerland have banned landfilling untreated waste.
The UK taxes biodegradable waste sent to landfill, and England set up a scheme for councils to trade landfill quotas.
The zero waste concept aims to minimise landfill volume.

definition.text: Municipal solid waste is everyday rubbish, the trash or garbage of items thrown away by the public.

facts.text: Its make-up varies greatly between places and over time; where recycling is well developed, what is left is mainly plastic film and non-recyclable packaging.
Most definitions leave out industrial, agricultural, medical and radioactive waste and sewage sludge.
Typical Chinese municipal waste is 55.9% food residue, 11.2% plastics and 8.5% paper.
The industry has four parts: recycling, composting, disposal and waste-to-energy incineration.
Waste hierarchies rank methods from most to least preferred: reduce and reuse, recycle or compost, recover energy, then treat and dispose.
It produces large amounts of methane, nearly 90% of which could be avoided with existing technologies.

title: Source separation of waste
article: Municipal solid waste#Waste handling and separation, storage and processing at the source

definition.text: Source separation means sorting waste into types, such as biodegradable, recyclable, residual and hazardous, where it is produced.

facts.text: It improves recycling, prevents contamination, allows composting and ensures hazardous waste is properly treated.
Separated and mixed wastes are processed at materials recovery facilities using hand sorting, screens, magnets and optical sorting.
Segregation, composting and recycling can cut methane emissions from municipal waste.

definition.text: Reuse means using items again, by repairing, gifting, refurbishing or lending them, instead of throwing them away.

facts.text: Reuse lengthens product life and reduces the need for fresh raw materials.
Online networks such as Freecycle list unwanted items for others to reuse, reducing landfill pollution.
Unlike recycling, it does not break items down into raw materials, which saves time, money, energy and resources.
Extending an item's use is preferable to recycling or disposal because it is the least energy-intensive option.

definition.text: Waste-to-energy is the generation of power from municipal waste, by burning it or by capturing landfill gas, pyrolysis or gasification.

facts.text: Older incinerators emitted many pollutants, but new rules and technology have greatly reduced this.
US rules in 1995 and 2000 cut dioxin emissions from such plants by over 99% below 1990 levels and mercury by over 90%.
Because waste contains food, wood and paper, burning it can partly count as bioenergy.

definition.text: Particulate matter is microscopic solid or liquid particles suspended in the air.

facts.text: Particles mixed with air are called an aerosol; they come from both natural and human sources.
Major components include wind-blown mineral dust, sea salt, organic matter and particles formed from gases such as SO2 and ammonia.
It is considered the most dangerous air pollution because particles reach deep into the lungs and travel in the blood to organs such as the brain.
There is no safe level of exposure, and airborne particulate matter is a Group 1 carcinogen.
Fine particles (PM2.5) are the leading environmental risk factor for early death worldwide.
Because many sources are human, it is a risk that policy can reduce, and many countries now set standards for it.
After the US Clean Air Act of 1970, combined emissions of criteria and precursor pollutants fell 79% from 1970 to 2024.

definition.text: Particles are grouped by diameter: coarse PM10 (10 micrometres or less), fine PM2.5 (2.5 micrometres or less) and ultrafine particles.

facts.text: Size is a key factor in how much harm a particle can do.
Coarse PM10 particles lodge in the nose, throat and upper airways.
Fine PM2.5 particles penetrate deep into the lungs, reaching the smallest airways and air sacs.
Across all causes of death, PM2.5 has more severe effects than PM10.

title: Health effects of particulate matter

definition.text: Breathing particulate matter is linked to disease throughout the body and to large numbers of early deaths.

facts.text: It contributes to stroke, heart disease, respiratory disease, many cancers and preterm birth, and to cognitive impairment.
Worldwide, PM2.5 exposure contributed to 7.9 million deaths in 2023: 4.9 million linked to outdoor and 2.8 million to household air pollution.
The link between particle pollution and premature deaths was first shown in the early 1970s; the 1993 Harvard Six Cities study established it firmly for cities.
Both short-term and long-term exposure cause harm.
In the EU, PM2.5 deaths fell 57% between 2005 and 2023, attributed to policies that cut primary PM2.5 emissions by 38%.
China's 2013 air pollution action plan cut annual average PM2.5 by a third by 2017, with fewer deaths.

notes: Death counts differ by study and year: the 2021 Global Burden of Disease gives 7.83 million deaths from outdoor PM2.5 (S:da0132b18423), while the 2023 figure gives 4.9 million outdoor; Air pollution page gives 4.7 million (S:20b96110021e). Not treated as conflicts because sources and years differ.

definition.text: The World Health Organization sets guideline limits for particle exposure, above which health risks rise.

facts.text: For PM2.5 the annual mean should not exceed 5 μg/m3 and the 24-hour mean 15 μg/m3.
For PM10 the annual mean should not exceed 15 μg/m3 and the 24-hour mean 45 μg/m3.
Under the 2021 guideline, 97% of the world's population is exposed to unsafe PM2.5 levels.

definition.text: The burden of particle pollution falls more heavily on non-White people and those living in poverty.

facts.text: Living near particle-emitting facilities raises PM2.5 exposure and rates of illness and death.
In the US, disparities for Black people are larger than income alone explains, and scholars link them to housing segregation.
About 1.6 billion people live near sources of PM2.5 and other toxins, 900 million of them near super-emitting facilities.

definition.text: Aerosols change Earth's climate by altering how much incoming sunlight and outgoing heat the planet keeps.

facts.text: They act directly, by scattering and absorbing radiation, and indirectly, by changing clouds, since cloud droplets form on particles.
The direct effect produces a net negative radiative forcing, that is, cooling.
Aerosol effects are the biggest source of uncertainty in climate predictions.
Soot is a strong absorber of radiation, while sea-salt particles only scatter it.

definition.text: Industries control particle emissions with dust collection systems such as cyclones, fabric filters, wet scrubbers and electrostatic precipitators.

facts.text: Particle emissions are highly regulated in most industrialised countries.
Fabric filters, or baghouses, are the most common in general industry.
Electrostatic precipitators charge particles and collect them on large charged plates.

definition.text: Nonpoint source pollution is diffuse contamination of water or air that does not come from a single identifiable source.

facts.text: It is often the combined effect of small amounts of pollutants gathered from a large area.
It contrasts with point source pollution, which comes from a single source.
It arises from land runoff, rain, deposition from the air, drainage and seepage, which makes tracing it to one source difficult.
Paved urban surfaces and farms that apply fertilizer and manure are major sources.
A smokestack is a point source, but its pollution, carried far and mixed with others, acts as nonpoint where it lands.
It is the leading cause of water pollution in the United States, mainly from farm runoff and altered waterways.

title: Types of nonpoint water pollutants
article: Nonpoint source pollution#Principal types (for water pollution)

definition.text: The main nonpoint water pollutants are sediment, nutrients, toxic chemicals and disease-causing pathogens.

facts.text: Sediment clouds water, cutting light for underwater plants and the fish and shellfish that depend on them.
Phosphorus and nitrogen are the two nutrients of most concern.
Heavy metals and compounds such as PCBs and DDT resist breakdown and persist in the environment.
Coliform bacteria in runoff are used as an indicator of water pollution rather than being a cause of disease.

definition.text: Nonpoint pollution is controlled by land practices that slow runoff and trap pollutants before they reach water.

facts.text: Grass buffer strips between paved areas and water let soil absorb pollutants first.
Retention ponds let contaminants in stormwater settle out and stay trapped.
Farmers use contour ploughing, mulching, crop rotation, perennial crops, riparian buffers and conservation tillage.
Agroforestry can also improve air quality by absorbing pollutants such as particulate matter.

title: Regulating nonpoint source pollution
article: Nonpoint source pollution#Regulation of Nonpoint Source Pollution in the United States

definition.text: Nonpoint pollution is hard to regulate because it has no single discharge point; US federal law leaves it largely to states and voluntary programs.

facts.text: Diffuse sources were excluded from the US Clean Water Act's permit programme for that reason.
State programmes rely on best management practices, seeking the least costly way to cut the most pollution.
A 2015 article found the Clean Water Act effective for point sources but not for nonpoint sources.
Since 1987 federal grants under section 319 have funded state nonpoint management programmes.

title: Environmental site assessment

definition.text: An environmental site assessment is a report on a property that identifies possible or existing contamination liabilities.

facts.text: The Phase I assessment is the first step of environmental due diligence and usually involves no sampling.
US demand rose sharply in the 1980s after court rulings made property owners liable for cleanup.
A Phase II assessment collects soil, water or building samples when Phase I suggests contamination is likely.

notes: Largely US-specific due-diligence practice; kept as a possible minor note for the brownfield entries.

title: Damage function
article: Economic analysis of climate change#Damage functions

definition.text: A relationship used in cost-benefit analysis that estimates the economic damage caused by an environmental change such as warming.

facts.text: Damage functions have been built for sea level rise, farm productivity and the effect of heat on labour productivity.
A common base form makes damages grow with the square of warming: 2 °C causes 4 times and 3 °C 9 times the damage of 1 °C.
Some versions add tipping points so damages speed up, or jump, once warming passes 2-3 °C.
Estimates of the social cost of carbon are highly sensitive to the damage function chosen, along with the discount rate.
A 2020 paper using an updated damage function found that around 2 °C of warming would be "optimal" in the DICE model.
Nicholas Stern argued that damage functions miss many of society's most important risks.
Damage functions are central to estimating the costs of climate-related hazards.
They have been built for sea level rise, farm productivity and the effect of heat on labour productivity.

contested_note: Critics such as Nicholas Stern argue standard damage functions leave out major risks, and updated functions change the 'optimal' warming results.
distinct_from: Global economic costs of climate change

definition.text: Incineration is a waste treatment process that burns the substances in waste, turning it into ash, flue gas and heat.

facts.text: Plants come in several designs, such as moving grate, fixed grate, rotary-kiln and fluidised bed; the moving grate is typical for municipal solid waste.
Heat can raise steam to drive a turbine; net output is about 2/3 MWh of electricity and 2 MWh of district heating per tonne of municipal waste.
Raw flue gas can carry particulate matter, heavy metals, dioxins, furans, sulfur dioxide and hydrochloric acid, so modern plants add flue gas cleaning.
Nearly all the carbon in the waste leaves as CO2; incinerating 1 ton of municipal waste yields about 1 ton of CO2.
Ash makes up 4 to 10% of the waste by volume and 15-20% by weight; fly ash is about 10-20% of it, and bottom ash can go to landfill or be recycled as construction aggregate.
Plant lifetimes of 25 to 30 years and the long contracts needed to recover investment can lock a municipality in.

title: Debate over waste incineration

definition.text: The use of incinerators for waste management is controversial, weighing the economic appeal of local industry against health and environmental risk.

facts.text: Supporters say it avoids landfill methane, saves landfill space where land is scarce, and replaces fossil power with partly biomass-based energy.
Supporters also note that in Europe the highest incineration rates generally go with top recycling performance.
Critics say fly ash concentrates ecotoxic heavy metals and needs specialized landfills, and that the waste hierarchy prefers prevention, reuse and recycling.
In the UK, the EU Landfill Directive led to the landfill tax and the Landfill Allowance Trading Scheme.

contested_note: Incineration is contested between business, regulators, activists and residents over health, recycling and lock-in.

definition.text: Black carbon is the light-absorbing form of elemental carbon left by pyrolysis or produced by incomplete combustion, as in soot.

facts.text: It forms from incomplete combustion of fossil fuels, biofuel and biomass and is fine particulate matter that causes premature death and disability.
About 20% of emissions come from biofuels, 40% from fossil fuels and 40% from open biomass burning.
Developed countries were once the main source, but control technologies since the 1950s shifted most emissions to developing countries.
Estimates say 640,000 to 4,900,000 premature deaths a year could be prevented with available mitigation measures.
In soils black carbon is typically 1 to 6% of organic carbon, and Terra preta soils hold about three times the organic matter of surrounding soils.

title: Black carbon and climate

definition.text: Black carbon warms the climate by absorbing sunlight, altering clouds and darkening snow and ice.

facts.text: The IPCC's 2007 report put direct forcing from fossil-fuel black carbon at +0.2 W/m2 and the snow and ice albedo effect at an additional +0.1 W/m2; later estimates rank it second after carbon dioxide.
Estimates of direct forcing range from the IPCC's +0.34 W/m2 (plus or minus 0.25) to 0.9 W/m2 by Ramanathan and Carmichael.
Because it stays in the air only weeks, cutting emissions may be the fastest way to slow near-term warming.
A 2013 study found gas flares contributed over 40% of black carbon deposited in the Arctic.

notes: Forcing estimates differ by source and definition (IPCC vs Ramanathan and Carmichael); listed as facts, not as a conflict.

definition.text: Black carbon can be cut with existing technology and national laws on particulate emissions.

facts.text: Developed nations reduced fossil-fuel black carbon by a factor of 5 or more since 1950, mainly to improve air quality and public health.
Small-scale sources such as domestic cooking may shift when affordable alternatives exist, while vehicles and coal boilers may need regulation.
Policy options include regulating slash-and-burn clearing, shore power for ships at port, and vehicle emissions tests with retrofitting such as particulate traps.

definition.text: Environmental remediation is the cleanup of hazardous substances: removing, treating or containing pollution in soil, groundwater and sediment.

facts.text: Waste can be removed and transported off-site for disposal, or contained by physical barriers such as slurry walls.
Regulations may require remediation before land is redeveloped, and voluntary cleanups can earn incentives, such as New York State's Brownfield Cleanup Program.
Assessment begins when a site is suspected contaminated, often with a Phase I Environmental Site Assessment guided by the site's history.
Cleanup standards differ: the US uses EPA Regional Screening Levels, Europe has the Dutch standards, and Canadian provinces set their own.
In the US a tax on polluting industries funds a Superfund for abandoned sites; elsewhere sites are often rezoned to higher uses so land value covers cleanup costs.
Remediation can face local resistance to rezoning; main impacts are noise, dust, odour and incremental health risk.

definition.text: Remediation technologies fall into ex-situ methods, which excavate or extract contaminated soil and groundwater for surface treatment, and in-situ methods, which treat contamination in place.

facts.text: Pump and treat draws up contaminated groundwater and purifies it, for petroleum usually through granular activated carbon.
In situ chemical oxidation injects strong oxidants such as hydrogen peroxide, ozone, potassium permanganate or persulfates.
Stabilization and solidification binds contaminants to stop their mobility, but has durability problems and cement CO2 emissions.
Bioremediation uses microorganisms, through biostimulation, bioaugmentation or natural attenuation, in situ or ex situ.
Nanoremediation uses nano-sized reactive agents that degrade organic contaminants or immobilize metals such as lead or arsenic.

definition.text: Incremental health risk is the added risk a nearby person faces from a remediation project or from the lack of one.

facts.text: It rests on carcinogenic and other effects and involves value judgements about the acceptable projected rate of increase in cancer.
The acceptable increase is 1 in 1,000,000 in some jurisdictions and 1 in 100,000 in others.

definition.text: Greenfield land is undeveloped land, farmed, landscaped or left natural, in an urban or rural area.

facts.text: It is usually agricultural or amenity land being considered for urban development, and gives a developer high freedom compared with built-up sites.
A developer may instead redevelop brownfield or greyfield land that was built on but left abandoned or underused.
